Cross-language Compatibility

Shared semantics, native return types, and reproducible workflows in R, Python, and Julia.

Compatibility contract

The R, Python, and Julia packages are separate implementations of the same taxonomic hierarchy distance. Version 0.7.0 preserves their core behavioral contract:

  • ordered lineages are compared through their continuous common prefix;
  • identical complete lineages receive distance zero;
  • distinct nodes receive \(1 / \operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA})\);
  • valid Taxonomicon nodes have distances in \((0,1]\), while disconnected inputs retain infinite distance as a defensive result;
  • unresolved lineages produce missing values in multi-taxon results;
  • ancestor–descendant pairs retain positive distance;
  • clade membership uses exact, case-insensitive matching;
  • the packaged reference data preserve the same component structure, taxa, order, values, and provenance.

Compatibility means equivalent scientific semantics and labeled results. It does not mean that every object has the same internal representation or printed appearance.

Equivalent basic workflow

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
library(taxodist)

taxa <- c(
  "Tyrannosaurus",
  "Velociraptor",
  "Triceratops",
  "Homo sapiens"
)

lineage <- get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")
pair <- taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
matrix <- distance_matrix(taxa, progress = FALSE)

pair$mrca
pair$distance
as.matrix(matrix)
import taxodist as td

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

lineage = td.get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")
pair = td.taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
matrix = td.distance_matrix(taxa, progress=False)

pair["mrca"]
pair["distance"]
matrix
using Taxodist

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

lineage = get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")
pair = taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
matrix = distance_matrix(taxa, progress=false)

pair.mrca
pair.distance
matrix

For lineages retrieved from the same Taxonomicon record and processed under the same version, the MRCA depth and distance should agree.

Function correspondence

Task Shared function
Resolve a name get_taxonomicon_id()
Search candidates taxo_search()
Retrieve a lineage get_lineage(), get_lineage_by_id()
Compare two nodes taxo_distance(), mrca()
Construct a matrix distance_matrix()
Compare a focal taxon focal_distances(), closest_relative()
Inspect lineages compare_lineages(), shared_clades(), taxo_path()
Test membership is_member(), filter_clade()
Check availability check_coverage(), lineage_depth()
Analyze a matrix taxo_cluster(), taxo_ordinate(), taxo_heatmap()
Manage the cache cache_info(), save_cache(), load_cache(), clear_cache()
Load reference data R: data(taxobase); Python and Julia: load_taxobase()

Argument names and defaults are matched where language conventions permit. All three implementations support verbose; progress reporting is available for matrix operations, with minor interface differences documented in the API reference.

Native object differences

Result R Python Julia
Lineage Character vector List of strings Vector{String}
Pairwise distance S3 list, class taxodist_result Dictionary Named tuple
Distance matrix Base R dist Labeled pandas.DataFrame TaxonomicDistanceMatrix
Coverage Named logical vector Boolean pandas.Series DataFrame
Closest/focal results Data frame, with S3 class for focal results pandas.DataFrame with attributes DataFrame or named tuple containing one
Taxonomic path Data frame, class taxodist_path pandas.DataFrame with attributes DataFrame
Clustering hclust inside taxodist_cluster SciPy linkage matrix inside a dictionary Clustering result inside a named tuple
Ordination coordinates Numeric matrix Labeled pandas.DataFrame DataFrame with a labeled source matrix
Cache Environment serialized to .rds Dictionary serialized to .pkl Dictionaries serialized to .json
Missing numeric value NA_real_ NaN NaN
Missing object NULL None nothing

These differences are intentional. They allow results to integrate naturally with each language rather than imitating the other language’s object system.

Pairwise result fields

All three implementations return the same named information from taxo_distance():

Field Meaning
distance Hierarchy distance
mrca Name of the MRCA
mrca_depth Depth of the MRCA
depth_a Complete depth of lineage A
depth_b Complete depth of lineage B
taxon_a First input label
taxon_b Second input label

R uses $, Python uses dictionary indexing, and Julia uses property access:

R:      result$mrca
Python: result["mrca"]
Julia:  result.mrca

Distance matrices

R stores only the lower triangle in a compact dist object. Convert it when a square matrix is required:

d <- distance_matrix(taxa)
m <- as.matrix(d)

Python returns the square labeled matrix directly:

d = td.distance_matrix(taxa)
m = d.to_numpy()

Julia returns a square labeled matrix type directly:

d = distance_matrix(taxa)
m = Matrix(d)
value = d["Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor"]

All three preserve input taxon order. Unresolved taxa remain labeled and have missing off-diagonal distances.

Clustering and ordination

The analysis results are semantically aligned but use different numerical ecosystems.

Clustering

R delegates to stats::hclust(), Python to SciPy, and Julia to Clustering.jl. With the same complete finite matrix and equivalent method, all three summarize the same dissimilarities, although internal merge representations and plotting defaults differ.

Ordination

All three implementations perform classical multidimensional scaling and return:

  • points;
  • the underlying dist or distance DataFrame;
  • GOF goodness-of-fit values;
  • eig eigenvalues.

Coordinate signs may differ between numerical implementations because eigenvectors are defined only up to sign. A sign reversal of an axis does not change the represented geometry or pairwise distances.

Compare geometry, not axis orientation

When validating ordinations across languages, compare eigenvalues and Euclidean distances among coordinates. Do not require every coordinate column to have the same sign.

Plotting and console output

R uses S3 methods such as print(), plot(), and summary(). Python and Julia expose explicit helpers such as plot_taxodist_cluster(), plot_taxodist_ord(), and summary_taxodist_ord().

Typography, plotting backends, colors, dendrogram orientation, and console formatting are not part of the cross-language compatibility contract. Scientific values, labels, and structural fields are.

Reference data parity

Release 0.7.0 distributes equivalent taxobase content in all three packages. Python and Julia load the neutral JSON reference into their native labeled containers.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
data(taxobase, package = "taxodist")

names(taxobase)
taxobase$metadata
labels(taxobase$statistical_matrix)
taxobase = td.load_taxobase()

taxobase.keys()
taxobase["metadata"]
taxobase["statistical_matrix"].index.tolist()
taxobase = load_taxobase()

keys(taxobase)
taxobase.metadata
taxobase.statistical_matrix.taxa

The corresponding objects preserve component names, taxon order, coverage values, pairwise metadata, lineage examples, general and statistical matrices, package version, and distance-definition metadata.

Cross-language matrix verification

A simple independent comparison can be performed through a neutral CSV representation.

Export from R

data(taxobase, package = "taxodist")

write.csv(
  as.matrix(taxobase$statistical_matrix),
  "taxobase-statistical-matrix.csv",
  quote = FALSE
)

Compare in Python

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import taxodist as td

from_r = pd.read_csv(
    "taxobase-statistical-matrix.csv",
    index_col=0,
)
from_python = td.load_taxobase()["statistical_matrix"]

assert from_r.index.tolist() == from_python.index.tolist()
assert from_r.columns.tolist() == from_python.columns.tolist()
assert np.allclose(
    from_r.to_numpy(),
    from_python.to_numpy(),
    rtol=0,
    atol=1e-12,
)

Compare in Julia

using DelimitedFiles
using Taxodist

raw = readdlm("taxobase-statistical-matrix.csv", ',', Any, '\n')
labels_from_r = String.(raw[2:end, 1])
matrix_from_r = Float64.(raw[2:end, 2:end])
from_julia = load_taxobase().statistical_matrix

@assert labels_from_r == from_julia.taxa
@assert all(isapprox.(
    matrix_from_r,
    Matrix(from_julia);
    rtol=0,
    atol=1e-12,
))

This checks labels, order, and numerical values without depending on language-specific serialization.

Version 0.7.0 validation and performance

Release 0.7.0 was revalidated with the same 52-taxon reference set in three order-rotated runs. Across languages, all 468 lineage audit records, resolved identifiers, finite-pair counts, and matrix checksums agreed.

Cached timings below are medians across the three runs; each timing summarizes 15 adaptively calibrated batches on the validation system.

Cached operation, \(n=52\) R Python Julia
Distance matrix 9.250 ms 4.358 ms 0.369 ms
Clustering 0.086 ms 0.124 ms 0.030 ms
Ordination 0.633 ms 0.675 ms 0.398 ms

At this size, Julia constructed the cached matrix 11.8 times faster than Python and 25.1 times faster than R. These values describe this implementation version, dataset, and validation system; they are not universal language benchmarks. Initial lineage retrieval was network-dominated and varied substantially between runs, so it should not be used to rank language performance.

Cache compatibility

Cache contents have the same conceptual keys—resolved IDs and lineages—but the files are intentionally not interchangeable:

  • R uses saveRDS() and .rds files;
  • Python uses pickle and .pkl files;
  • Julia uses JSON and .json files.

Do not rename one format to imitate another. For a cross-language archival record, export resolved numeric IDs and lineages to a neutral format such as CSV or JSON.

Untrusted Python cache files

Only load .pkl files from trusted sources. Python’s pickle format can execute code during deserialization.

Live retrieval may differ over time

The packages query an external website. Two runs can differ if they occur at different times, resolve different homonyms, encounter different network responses, or use different package versions.

For reproducible comparisons:

  1. use the same taxodist version;
  2. query the same numeric Taxonomicon IDs;
  3. record the retrieval date;
  4. verify lineage equality before comparing distances;
  5. save language-specific caches when live records must be retained;
  6. use taxobase for fixed examples and regression tests.

What compatibility does not guarantee

The project does not guarantee:

  • byte-identical serialized files;
  • identical console messages;
  • identical plot appearance;
  • identical internal clustering arrays;
  • identical eigenvector signs;
  • identical live results obtained from different source revisions.

It does guarantee a shared versioned definition and aims to preserve equivalent labels, distances, MRCA logic, edge-case handling, and reference data.
